news.title: Business News | Indian Stock Markets Closed Today for Dussehra, Trading to Resume on Wednesday
news.text:
Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 20 (ANI): Domestic stock markets will remain closed on Tuesday on account of Dussehra, with regular trading scheduled to resume on Wednesday, October 21.

The National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) have included Dussehra in their trading holiday calendars for 2026. Trading in the equity, equity derivatives, currency and securities lending and borrowing (SLB) segments will remain suspended for the day.

Also Read | Donald Trump Open to Vladimir Putin-Xi Jinping Talks on Ukraine War.

Meanwhile, trading on the Multi Commodity Exchange of India (MCX) will remain suspended during the morning session before resuming in the evening, enabling commodity trading to continue later in the day.

The holiday follows a weak session on Monday, when domestic equities came under selling pressure amid weakness in private bank stocks, corporate earnings that fell short of expectations and rising crude oil prices.

Also Read | Virender Sehwag Birthday Special: Celebrating India’s Fearless Opener As ‘Sultan of Multan’ Turns 48.

The BSE Sensex declined 876.37 points, or 1.17 per cent, to close at 73,852.90, while the Nifty 50 fell 257.20 points, or 1.11 per cent, to settle at 22,888.95.

Selling was widespread across sectors, with the Nifty PSU Bank index emerging as the only major sectoral index to end in positive territory, gaining 2.41 per cent. The Nifty IT index fell 1.56 per cent, while the Nifty FMCG index declined 1.40 per cent.

Vikram Kasat, Chief Business Officer – Advisory and Dealing at PL Capital, said weakness in private banks, disappointing earnings relative to expectations and cautious global sentiment had intensified profit-booking. He added that markets could remain volatile as investors track corporate earnings, crude oil prices and currency stability.

Oil prices remain an important factor for market sentiment. Brent crude was trading at USD 109.66 per barrel at the time of filing this report, up 0.10 per cent, keeping concerns over imported inflation and corporate costs in focus.

Investors are expected to monitor corporate earnings, movements in crude oil prices and global market cues when domestic equity trading resumes. (ANI)

Listen to this article Share France imposes curfews after riots and looting French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of Paris and several other cities after days of rioting and looting, as the government faces mounting pressure to restore order. Police announced restrictions between 23:00 and 06:00 local time in Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district in central Paris.

Authorities have also banned unauthorised gatherings in parts of the capital and introduced varying restrictions in Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice, Lyon and Lille. Prime Minister officials said local mayors would be empowered to impose curfews where necessary, although the government had not specified all the locations affected.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted that police had “lost control” in some cities, drawing criticism from opposition politicians over preparations for the unrest. More than 2,500 people have been arrested, while about 1,000 police officers have been injured. One demonstrator reportedly lost a hand after a police crowd-control grenade exploded.

The protests began last month with students demanding better school conditions but have expanded to include wider economic and social grievances, attracting trade unions and other groups. The escalation presents a challenge for President Emmanuel Macron’s government as it seeks to contain the violence while addressing public discontent.

Helen Haines, an independent Australian member of parliament, is critically ill in hospital after being struck by a car outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, Victoria. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the incident appeared to have been deliberate, although investigators were still working to establish the motive.

Police said Haines, 65, was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at about 15:35 local time on Monday. A 43-year-old man was detained at the scene by a passerby, and police said a knife was found in the vehicle. Haines was initially taken to a local hospital before being airlifted to Melbourne for further treatment.

Victoria Police said they were investigating whether the incident was intentional and that there was no indication of an ongoing threat to the community. Counter-terrorism police are involved in the investigation, although authorities have not publicly established a terrorism link.

Albanese condemned political violence, saying there was no place for it in a democracy. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 over the past year, renewing concerns about the safety of elected representatives.

More than 50 security personnel have been killed and about 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a training camp in Yemen’s central province of Shabwa, local authorities said. The attack targeted al Alam camp near Ataq, which was being used to train recruits for security forces and the police.

A spokesman for the Saudi backed Yemeni armed forces said the Houthis fired three ballistic missiles at the camp. The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al Alimi, condemned what he called a “criminal attack” and promised a firm response. The Houthis said they had targeted what they described as Saudi enemy concentrations.

The strike comes as Yemen’s civil war intensifies. In early October, pro-government forces launched an offensive to retake territory held by the Houthis, with support from a Saudi led coalition. They regained areas along the Red Sea coast overlooking the strategically important Bab al Mandab Strait.

Fighting continues around the government controlled city of Taiz and in Marib and al Jawf provinces. The Houthis have also launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in response to coalition air strikes, raising concerns that the conflict could further destabilise the region.

Barack Obama has criticised a federal investigation involving Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, describing it as “so appalling” and accusing the Trump administration of targeting an elected official for criticising the president. The White House rejected claims that the inquiry was politically motivated.

US media reports said the investigation concerns Omar’s immigration and citizenship history, including questions about her age when she arrived in the United States in 1995. Homeland security agents searched her Washington home last week as part of the inquiry. Omar, who was born in Somalia, moved to the US with her family as a child.

Obama argued that Omar’s father became a naturalised US citizen when she was 17, which he said made her eligible for citizenship under the law. He warned that pursuing an elected official on what he described as an unsubstantiated theory could set a precedent for future administrations to target political opponents.

Lauren Bis, White House spokeswoman denied that President Donald Trump had weaponised the Justice Department against his critics. She said the department was focused on restoring law and order and protecting Americans. The investigation’s allegations have not been established in court.

Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 31 percent, its lowest level across his two presidential terms, as Americans express concern about rising petrol prices ahead of the November 3 congressional elections, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found. The four day survey closed on Monday.

The poll found that 47 percent of registered voters would support Democrats if congressional elections were held immediately, compared with 35 percent who would vote for Republicans. The 12 percentage point Democratic advantage was the widest recorded during the current election cycle, suggesting growing dissatisfaction with the president and his party.

Republicans face the possibility of losing control of the House of Representatives or the Senate, either of which would complicate Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his term. The poll’s findings indicate that economic concerns, particularly fuel costs, could influence voting decisions.

However, the nationwide generic ballot question does not capture differences between individual states and congressional districts. Republicans retain structural advantages in some contests, meaning the national polling lead does not guarantee that Democrats will take control of either chamber.

Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s chief international anchor, will leave the network next year after 43 years, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters. Her departure comes as CNN enters a new ownership era following Skydance’s takeover of Warner Bros Discovery.

Amanpour will end her daily programmes across CNN and PBS at the end of this year. She is expected to continue hosting a weekly CNN programme through May and work on the transition until June. Her first major assignment was covering the Gulf War, and she later reported on conflicts in Bosnia, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran.

David Ellison, Skydance chief executive has faced criticism over his stewardship of CBS News, which is now under the same corporate ownership as CNN. Mark Thompson, CNN chief and Bari Weiss, CBS News editor-in-chief have retained their positions, reporting to Ellison and co chief executive Ynon Kreiz.

Lawmakers have accused Ellison of tailoring CBS News coverage to favour Trump, placing renewed attention on editorial independence under the new ownership. Amanpour’s departure marks a significant change for CNN’s international reporting, where she has become one of the network’s most recognisable journalists.

A Kenyan court has convicted preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 others of murder over the deaths of 190 children and an adult in one of the world’s worst cult related tragedies in recent history. The verdict was delivered on Monday, more than three years after authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie and his Good News International Church operated a doomsday sect whose followers were instructed to starve themselves and their children to reach heaven before the world ended. Mackenzie denied forcing victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence. He and the other convicted defendants are due to be sentenced on November 6.

The case has drawn widespread attention in Kenya and raised questions about how Mackenzie continued operating despite coming to the attention of authorities in 2017. Police searched his premises that year, and authorities shut down his church in 2019 before he relocated to Shakahola Forest, according to police.

The ruling brought some relief to relatives of the victims. Francis Wanje, who lost eight family members, including two grandchildren, told Reuters that the judgment strengthened his confidence in the judiciary. Mackenzie’s lawyer, Lawrence Obonyo, said he had been instructed to appeal.

Robert Kabera, a former Rwandan army sergeant major who became a vocal critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda. His body was discovered on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend, and Ugandan police said his head had not been recovered.

Kabera, 50, had fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied, and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution. His family said he had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45km outside Kampala before his death. His widow, Jeanne d’Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told the BBC that she feared for the safety of herself and their children.

His death has renewed concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living abroad. In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief and co founder of the opposition Rwanda National Congress, was found dead in a Johannesburg hotel. The RNC has called for a thorough investigation into Kabera’s killing and for those responsible to be brought to justice.

At least nine members of Libya’s Anti Threat Security Agency have been killed and several others wounded in a mortar blast during a training exercise in Zawiya, west of Tripoli, local media reported. The explosion occurred late on Sunday during an exercise involving the security force.

Libya Alahrar television reported that the blast involved an 82mm mortar round. The Anti Threat Security Agency operates under the UN recognised Government of National Unity led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah. Authorities had not issued an immediate public statement confirming the casualties.

Zawiya lies about 40km west of Tripoli and is home to Libya’s largest operating oil refinery. The city has also experienced repeated clashes between rival armed groups, reflecting persistent insecurity despite efforts to maintain a unified national government.

The incident highlights the risks facing security personnel in a country where armed factions continue to wield significant influence. Further details about the cause of the explosion and the number of injured personnel were not immediately available.

Egypt has said it is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with support to defend its security and stability as attacks by Yemen’s Iran aligned Houthis intensify. The announcement could mark a significant escalation in the regional conflict, which has expanded since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

President Abdel Fattah al Sisi requested an urgent parliamentary session to authorise military assistance if Saudi Arabia asks for it. A vote had been expected on Sunday, but two lawmakers and local media reports said discussions would continue on Monday. The presidency did not specify what form any assistance might take.

The Saudi led coalition supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while the Houthis control the capital, Sanaa, and much of the country’s north. Fighting between the two sides has intensified in recent weeks, opening another front in the wider conflict involving Iran and its regional allies.

Any Egyptian military involvement could broaden the war and increase pressure on regional security and energy supplies. The conflict has already disrupted global energy markets and pushed oil prices higher, raising concerns about further economic consequences if hostilities spread.

Gabon’s government says findings from its public debt audit remain under review by the International Monetary Fund and could be revised, as the country seeks a new financing programme. A government circular issued on Monday said Libreville was targeting a draft agreement with the IMF by the end of 2026.

Gabon requested a new programme in March and launched the audit in June to establish the scale of public debt, particularly domestic arrears. Preliminary findings published in September suggested total debt was lower than previously estimated. The latest circular, however, showed total arrears had risen to 1,198.8 billion CFA francs, equivalent to about $2.06 billion, by June 2026, up from 1,094.6 billion CFA francs at the end of 2025.

External arrears reached 437.3 billion CFA francs, or about $752 million. These included 176.7 billion CFA francs owed to China Exim and 92.4 billion CFA francs to multilateral creditors. Arrears to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, part of the World Bank Group, had also reappeared after Gabon cleared them in March 2025.

An IMF mission is expected to visit Gabon after discussions at the Fund’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, although no date has been announced. The government cautioned that an agreement within its targeted timeframe was not guaranteed. Gabon’s previous Extended Fund Facility programme expired in July 2024 after completing only two reviews.

news.title: Business News | India-New Zealand FTA Takes Effect Today, Aims to Boost Exports and Investment
news.text:
New Delhi [India], October 20 (ANI): The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) comes into effect on Tuesday, giving Indian exporters duty-free access across the New Zealand market and opening opportunities to expand trade, attract investment and strengthen agricultural cooperation between the two countries.

The agreement is expected to benefit labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, apparel, leather and footwear, where tariffs of up to 10 per cent will be eliminated from the outset. Engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, machinery, chemicals and agricultural products are among the other sectors expected to gain from improved market access, according to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

Also Read | Donald Trump Open to Vladimir Putin-Xi Jinping Talks on Ukraine War.

Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Monday said New Zealand's commitment to facilitate USD 20 billion in investments into India under the agreement could support manufacturing, infrastructure, services and employment.

"New Zealand's commitment to facilitate USD 20 billion in investment into India holds immense potential to strengthen manufacturing, infrastructure, services & innovation, supporting enterprise & employment," Goyal said in a post on X.

Also Read | Virender Sehwag Birthday Special: Celebrating India’s Fearless Opener As ‘Sultan of Multan’ Turns 48.

Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said the agreement was designed to build a long-term economic partnership beyond tariff reductions and access to markets.

"These ties are not only about market access and having more exports to each other," Agrawal said, highlighting the focus on deeper economic cooperation.

The agreement covers market access across 70 per cent of tariff lines, while India has kept 30 per cent of its tariff lines excluded. For products covered under the agreement, New Zealand will eliminate duties immediately on 30 per cent of tariff lines, with reductions on the remaining lines phased over up to 10 years or implemented through tariff cuts and tariff-rate quotas.

Bilateral trade in goods and services currently stands at USD 2.4 billion. Both countries have set a target of doubling trade to NZD 7 billion, equivalent to around Rs 35,000 crore, by 2030.

The agreement also provides for faster customs clearance, with cargo to be cleared within 48 hours and express and perishable consignments within 24 hours. Digital certification and self-certification of rules of origin for eligible exporters are also envisaged.

In agriculture, the two countries will launch a productivity partnership using New Zealand's expertise in precision agriculture and related technologies. Cooperation will focus on improving farm productivity and incomes, including through Centres of Excellence for apples, kiwifruit and honey. Sensitive sectors, including dairy, will remain protected under the agreement.

Signed on April 27 and ratified on September 21, the FTA also aims to diversify India's export markets and strengthen supply-chain links as both countries work towards their 2030 trade target. (ANI)

news.title: Unresolved Border Dispute Continues to Strain India-China Relations
news.text:
The unresolved border dispute remains a central security concern and the principal obstacle in India-China relations which are still short of their pre-2020 status quo despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi last month for the BRICS summit prompting speculation that both countries are moving toward a reset, a report has highlighted.

India has sought to stabilise ties and manage differences with China since the 2020 Galwan clashes with the efforts gaining momentum due to US President Donald Trump’s increasingly hostile policies toward India and much of Asia, a report in The Diplomat highlighted.

However, Xi’s New Delhi visit for the BRICS Summit in September and the bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi should not be mistaken for an alignment of interests, the report cautioned.

“The resumption of high-level dialogue, leadership meetings, and direct connectivity are important developments. Another Galwan-like border confrontation would carry heavy domestic costs and could be difficult to recover from. Preventing a recurrence of such violence is a priority. But this does not require India to reconsider its position on the underlying differences,” wrote Sana Hashmi, a fellow at the Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation.

“It is also important to note that India never abandoned dialogue with China after Galwan. Keeping communication channel open has remained part of its approach, even as tensions persisted along the border. The latest meetings continue that policy; they do not demonstrate that the relationship or India’s approach to it has fundamentally changed,” Hashmi mentioned.

The report mentioned that China’s recent statement that it does not recognise the Union Territory of Ladakh, underlines the depth of the disagreement.

“There is little basis for expecting a reset while the two sides remain so far apart on territorial issues. Nor is the border the only source of friction. China’s relationship with Pakistan and the persistent trade imbalance remain contentious issues, too. There is little evidence of progress on any of these fundamental differences,” it added.

The Diplomat report stated that the Galwan clashes changed India’s view of and threat perception from China and raised serious questions about the viability of the existing arrangements in ensuring peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).

“High-level meetings can help manage tensions for the time being, but they cannot substitute for progress on the ground. India is also unlikely to return to its previous position on the One China policy without some reference to, or assurance regarding, a corresponding One India policy from Beijing. Such an assurance appears unlikely in the foreseeable future,” Hashmi opined.

“Just a couple of years ago, a meeting between Xi and Modi on Indian soil seemed difficult to imagine. That is one of the reasons why their meeting drew so much attention. But it has not changed the scope or nature of the issues dividing the two countries. For now, both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved. Until those differences are addressed, dialogue may keep the relationship from deteriorating further, but it will not put China-India ties on the path to a reset,” the expert added.

During their meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, PM Modi had reiterated to Xi Jinping that India and China should show sensitivity to each other’s core concerns and be guided by mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity.

Both leaders had emphasised that “differences should not become disputes” and reaffirmed that the two countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties.

“The two leaders welcomed the steady progress in India-China bilateral relations since their last meeting in Tianjin in August 2025. They reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties. Differences should not become disputes. Prime Minister highlighted that both sides must be guided by three mutuals- mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest,” read a statement issued by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) after the meeting.

news.title: Donald Trump interrupted five times at key rally before warning 'US may leave Europe'
news.text: President Donald Trump was interrupted five times as he took to the stage in Kansas, where he claimed the demonstrators' parents "slap them around". Running roughly an hour late, Trump faced his first disruption just moments into his speech while urging his supporters to "pretend" he's on the ballot. The audience reacted with anger, some booing while others launched into chants of "U-S-A." Trump then told his supporters : "Now, he goes home to mum and dad, they slap him around, and they say, 'I voted for that man.'" This comes after Trump unveiled striking 'red' hair which 'looks like squirrel on his head'. Within minutes, Trump was stopped for a second time. The president responded quickly, saying "there goes another one" and labelling them "paid protesters.", reports the Mirror US . He went on: "It's actually very dangerous. I can tell by the voice, they get paid. Whatever you do, get out and vote so we can get rid of idiots like that. It never ends." Trump then embarked on a rant about the Paris riots, claiming the French had "treasonously imported millions and millions of third world migrants". However, his supporters were distracted by another heckler from the opposite side of the venue - with those positioned behind Trump seen looking off to the right rather than concentrating on the president. Shaking his head with clear contempt, Trump observed: "So two-and-a-half people did that and tomorrow the headline will be 'Trump had to go through massive protest'." The event settled momentarily as Trump eventually hit his stride during the address, but he was compelled to stop for a fourth time as the crowd reacted angrily to yet another protester. As they were led away, Trump stated: "You know the amazing thing, these kids get paid $250 for that and then they get arrested and ruin their whole lives." That turned out not to be the last disruption, as Trump was interrupted for a fifth time while discussing "crooked Joe Biden" and Barack Obama. The exasperated crowd started booing once again before launching into chants, while a clearly irritated Trump stopped talking and started pumping his fist. "By the way, you have great law enforcement," he noted as the fifth person was ejected from the venue. Trump is keeping up his gruelling schedule of back-to-back rallies with his appearance in Kansas. His trip to the Sunflower State comes after a draining itinerary that's taken him across the country, with stops in Alaska, Arizona and Alabama, as well as Texas, Tennessee and Ohio. One person on X remarked, "I guess that's different than the paid audience behind him." Another stated, "Hope he doesn't have them beat on like the lady in Youngstown last week! "The protesters are there for free. It's his supporters who are recruited on Craigslist and paid to be there," a third person alleged. The president's comments arrive as the midterms approach and the Democrats are widely expected to gain control of the House of Representatives. Trump's address then turned to the ongoing riots in France, during which he warned the US would "leave" Europe . The president stated: "We stand with Europe despite its flaws, its weaknesses, and hopefully its temporary loss of direction - but if they don't soon find their way, we will have NO CHOICE but to leave." The remarks follow Trump's assertion that the protests and unrest have been caused by mass migration, claiming he told Macron to close the borders 'a long time ago'.
news.summary: President Donald Trump faced five interruptions at his Kansas rally, where he branded protesters 'paid' and claimed their parents 'slap them around' before warning the US could leave Europe over the France riots

news.title: New Mexico Republican Rejects Trump’s Push to Rename State
news.text: Gregg Hull, Republican candidate for governor in New Mexico, balked at President Donald Trump's push to rename the state as "New America." In a post to Truth Social earlier on Monday, the president said, "New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" He said the name change would add great "value and prestige," adding that incomes and home values would rise. "Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!" Trump said. Hull responded to the president's idea in a post to X on Monday night, saying in part that he stands by his original statement that "New Mexico does not need a new name." This is not the first time the president has floated the idea. In September, he posted a picture depicting the state with Mexico crossed out and America written below. During his time in office, the president has also rebranded the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America. He has also floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait" amid the country's ongoing war with Iran. When reached about Hull's remarks, the White House referred Newsweek to the president's comments. What To Know Hull added in his post on X that the state's identity is rooted in rich culture, beautiful landscape and the resilience of its people. "That identity is never up for negotiation. EVER," Hull said. He added that the people of New Mexico are focused on good-paying jobs, taxes and an economy that works for families, energy independence and relief from rising costs. "That is where my focus is, and that is what the campaign is about," Hull concluded. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump lost New Mexico during the 2024 presidential election to then-Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 6 percent. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. Gas prices in New Mexico, meanwhile, are above the national average, according to AAA. On Monday, a gallon of regular gasoline there cost $4.3465 compared to the national average of $4.2953. Last month, an article in the Albuquerque Journal ripped into the president's proposal of renaming the state, calling it, "so elementary and such low-hanging fruit, the biggest surprise was that it took so long for him to make it." In the op-ed by journalist Ryan Boetel he continued, saying, "My advice: Don't waste your breath," he said. "When immature people get frustrated, there's a tried and tired tactic of acting more and more obnoxious to get a rise out of someone to bring them down to their level." MapQuest, which recently defied Trump on his renaming of Lake Ontario, reacted to the moment on X Monday, saying, "Hey, boo. @NewMexico" New Mexico Lawmakers React to Trump's Proposal Senator Ben Ray Lujan, a Democrat, said that New Mexico's name carries history and will remain intact long after Trump is out of office. "New Mexico’s name dates back hundreds of years, long before the United States even existed. It carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are. We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico," Lujan said on X Monday. news.title: Gavin Newsom says ex-wife Kimberly Guilfoyle's scandal is 'unfortunate' as he addresses her being ousted as ambassador to Greece for the first time
news.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom called his ex-wife Kimberly Guilfoyle's unceremonious exit from her position as ambassador to Greece 'unfortunate' in brief remarks while campaigning for Democrats on Monday.

Newsom, who was married to the now-former ambassador from 2001 to 2005, was asked about her downfall on Monday.

'Recently, your ex wife, Kimberly Guilfoyle was involved in a scandal and pushed out of her ambassadorship,' a CBS News reporter asked. 'Could you please share what your reaction was to that news?' 

'I don't know enough about it,' he told CBS News. 'I haven't talked to her in a while, and I just wish her the best.'

He then added that the situation is 'unfortunate.' 

The Democrat's remarks come one week after Guilfoyle, 57, was forced to resign in the aftermath of exclusive Daily Mail reporting that she was the subject of an Inspector General (IG) investigation over her partying lifestyle and excessive spending habits in Athens.

A source close to the ambassador told the Daily Mail that Guilfoyle did not accept the news well, 'making excuses, saying how unfair it was.'

In a statement posted to X, Guilfoyle insisted the allegations against her are ‘false’, and vowed to ‘vigorously defend’ her name and reputation as her time as US Ambassador to Greece comes to an end.

'I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,' Guilfoyle wrote. 'While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end.'

Guilfoyle went on to thank President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio and pointed to her record in Athens, while pledging to remain a ‘loyal supporter’ of the president and his MAGA mission.

But the Daily Mail exclusively revealed that the State Department officially opened a probe into complaints about Guilfoyle's allegedly 'tyrannical' leadership and lavish corporate perks at the US Embassy in Athens.

Three sources said the IG is looking into allegations surrounding Guilfoyle's potential substance abuse, use of private planes and helicopters, close relationship with an energy and construction company, improper gift acceptance and more. 

Guilfoyle was also facing allegations that she solicited a $100,000 donor payment toward personal credit card debt in exchange for political access, and other accusations of unethical behavior. 

Trump-world insider Eric Deters, who Guilfoyle reportedly asked for a six-figure payment, even told the Daily Mail that she recruited Deters' wife and her friend to secretly sneak alcohol to her during a political festival, acting 'like a high schooler' hiding booze from her parents.

When the event ended, Guilfoyle insisted on packing up all the leftover catered VIP food to take home, Deters said.

He added that she begged him to compliment her in front of Donald Trump Jr, her former fiancé, in the hope of 'winning back his favor.' 

Guilfoyle's affinity for Champagne and parties have widely been documented, and insiders urged her to be on good behavior after she was tapped to be Trump's Greek Ambassador, cautioning that an assignment amid Aegean islands and endless summers wasn't a green light for nonstop partying.

Her lawyers since have hit back at the allegations, insisting the dispute with Deters concerns unpaid work rather than an attempt to sell access to the administration.

In a statement, they said he owed her approximately $150,000 for speaking engagements and consulting work performed in 2024 and early 2025.

But following the allegations, both Democrats and Republicans spoke out about the accusations against Guilfoyle, with Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso saying the reports were 'very troubling' and 'concerning.'

He added that he expected the State Department to conduct an investigation into the ambassador, before noting that ‘the Senate Foreign Relations Committee will have oversight and look into that as well.’ 

Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees also urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to investigate the claims. 

'If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,' wrote Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the top House Foreign Affairs Democrat.

The president also made clear the former fiancée to his son was never a member of his family.

'She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago,' Trump said dismissively.

Guilfoyle began dating Donald Trump Jr in 2018, months after his split from his wife Vanessa, and the pair soon became one of the most recognizable double acts in MAGA world.

Don Jr proposed on New Year’s Eve 2020, but the wedding never happened. After six years together, the relationship quietly unraveled, and by late 2024 he had moved on with Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson.

news.title: World News | US Advises Americans in Saudi Arabia to Follow Civil Defence Alerts Amid Houthi Attacks
news.text:
Riyadh [Saudi Arabia], October 20 (ANI): The United States has advised its citizens in Saudi Arabia to follow Civil Defence alerts and exercise extreme caution amid heightened security concerns following reported missile and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attacks on airports in the Kingdom.

In a security alert issued on October 19, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia urged American citizens to remain vigilant and follow safety instructions issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence through cellular broadcasts.

Also Read | Donald Trump Open to Vladimir Putin-Xi Jinping Talks on Ukraine War.

“U.S. citizens are reminded to follow the guidance of national alerts released by Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence via cellular broadcast,” the embassy stated.

The advisory warned of potential further attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and travel disruptions, urging Americans to exercise extreme caution while using airports in the Kingdom.

Also Read | Donald Trump Urges France To 'Close the Borders' As Violent Clashes Trigger Curfews and Mass Arrests.

The alert comes amid heightened regional tensions, with Houthi military spokesperson Brigadier General Yahya Saree claiming that Saudi forces carried out 110 airstrikes and missile attacks across several Yemeni governorates over a 24-hour period, resulting in more than 30 casualties, mostly women and children. The claims have not been independently verified in the supplied information.

According to the US Embassy, operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh remained suspended, while King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam continued operating amid some delays and cancellations.

The embassy advised travellers to verify flight departure information directly with airlines and airports, adding that private cars, trains and buses could serve as alternatives to air travel.

All land border crossings, including the King Fahd Causeway connecting Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, remained operational. Highways and roads in and around Riyadh, Jeddah and Dhahran were also operational, the advisory stated.

The US mission said American government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorisation from the Chief of Mission to use any airport in the Kingdom following the recent missile and UAV attacks.

It also highlighted restrictions on US government employees travelling within 20 miles of the Yemen border and requirements for special authorisation to visit the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif.

The embassy further warned American citizens against photographing or sharing information related to missile interceptions, drone activity and impact sites, citing Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Interior.

“Filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones, and their impact sites, exposes you to legal liability,” the advisory quoted the ministry as warning.

The embassy urged Americans to avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, monitor local media, follow instructions from Saudi authorities and remain alert at locations publicly associated with the United States.

It also advised citizens to keep their mobile phones charged and enrol in the State Department's Smart Traveller Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates and facilitate communication with the embassy during emergencies.

Regular and emergency consular services for US citizens remain available, the advisory said. (ANI)

news.title: Business News | High Bond Yields Could More Than Double Drag on US Growth in 2027: Goldman Sachs
news.text:
New Delhi [India], October 20 (ANI): Persistently high bond yields could more than double their drag on US economic growth in 2027, while rising borrowing costs threaten to weaken business investment and test the resilience of financial markets, according to a report by Goldman Sachs.

The report estimated that higher interest rates would reduce US economic growth by around 0.2 percentage points in 2027 under its baseline scenario. If borrowing costs remain near current levels, however, the drag could rise to just over 0.5 percentage points, more than twice the baseline impact.

Also Read | Donald Trump Open to Vladimir Putin-Xi Jinping Talks on Ukraine War.

Goldman Sachs economists expect the US economy to grow close to its estimated potential rate of 2.3 per cent in 2027. However, the report cautioned that this outlook could face greater pressure if bond yields remain elevated, with higher financing costs affecting housing, consumption and business investment.

“If rates were to remain at current levels, we estimate the drag would more than double, rising to just over 0.5 pp," the report said.

Also Read | Virender Sehwag Birthday Special: Celebrating India’s Fearless Opener As ‘Sultan of Multan’ Turns 48.

The report also highlighted concerns raised by Mark Zandi, Chief Economist of Moody’s Analytics, who described the US economy as vulnerable rather than resilient and views the “distribution of possible outcomes as very flat and heavily skewed toward darker tail scenarios,” the report said.

He put the odds of existing vulnerabilities pushing the economy "completely off the rails" at around one in three.

"The underlying labour market and household fundamentals point to very tenuous growth," Zandi added, citing weak hiring and stagnant or declining real wage growth that could weigh on household purchasing power.

The pressure from higher rates could extend beyond economic growth. Goldman Sachs estimated that higher refinancing costs could reduce business investment growth by around 0.3 percentage points in 2027 and subsequent years. That impact could more than double if borrowing rates remain near current levels, the report said.

At the same time, investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure has remained resilient despite higher interest rates and input costs. Goldman Sachs strategists expect AI-related capital expenditure to maintain a healthy pace in 2027, although the report flagged risks from rising leverage and the growing links between investment and financing across the AI sector.

The report noted that global bond yields had climbed to multi-decade highs even as economic growth and financial markets remained broadly resilient. However, further increases in yields or sustained volatility could test that resilience, particularly if inflation pressures prevent borrowing costs from easing.

The outlook for 2027 will therefore depend partly on whether yields moderate or remain elevated enough to deepen the pressure on economic activity and corporate investment, the report said. (ANI)

news.title: Palestinian Activist Appeals To US Supreme Court Over Trump Deportation Push
news.text: Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil on Monday asked the US Supreme Court to overturn a ruling that opened the door for President Donald Trump's administration to re-arrest and deport the Palestinian activist.Khalil's lawyers asked the justices to take up his case after the Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that federal immigration law barred a lower-court judge from ordering his release from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.Khalil was among the most prominent foreign students to be arrested last year as the Trump administration pursued a campaign to detain and deport noncitizens who engaged in pro-Palestinian activism on college campuses. His lawyers say the Supreme Court should make clear immigration law does not prevent noncitizens from pursuing cases arguing they have been detained to punish them for speech that is protected by the US Constitution's First Amendment."If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech," Khalil told reporters on Monday.If the 3rd Circuit's decision is allowed to stand, Khalil faces the prospect of arrest and deportation, after the Board of Immigration Appeals in April rejected his challenge to an immigration judge's order that he be removed to Algeria or Syria.A lower court order barring him from being re-detained remains in place for now until the Supreme Court rules. Immigration agents arrested him in March 2025 in the lobby of his university residence in Manhattan despite being a lawful permanent resident, or green-card holder. news.title: Trump Says America Could Mirror France if Republicans Lose Midterms
news.text: President Donald Trump invoked France in a warning Monday about what he claimed could happen in the United States if Democrats prevail in the midterm elections, telling supporters to “look at what’s happening in France” as he urged them to preserve Republican control of Congress. Speaking at a rally in Park City, Kansas, near Wichita, for Republican Senator Roger Marshall, Trump referred to the current protests in France and described the country as being damaged by immigration and unrest. He told the crowd that when they see “burning steeples and raging fires in France,” they should remember that “is what the radical Democrats want to do to America.” Trump’s comments come after nationwide protests in France over affordability and public services spilled into violence in some cities, including looting, fires and clashes with police. The president did not provide evidence that Democrats want violence or destruction in the United States. Newsweek reached out to the Democratic National Convention by email Monday night for comment. His appearance came 15 days before the November 3 election as Marshall faces an unexpectedly competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the Kansas Senate race a toss-up, while NBC News characterizes it as competitive but leaning Republican. Trump’s remarks came during an intensive Republican push to mobilize voters as control of Congress remains at stake. The battle for Congress is playing out largely on Republican-held terrain, according to NBC News, which says Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to take control. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also taken their campaign efforts into states and districts where Republican candidates are facing difficult contests. The Associated Press reported earlier this month that Trump launched what he called a 32-day campaign blitz while Vance also hit the campaign trail. Republican groups spent more than $740 million on congressional contests from Labor Day through October 14, including at least $220 million from Trump-linked groups, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. CNBC reported that Republicans were increasingly directing resources toward states including Kansas, Texas and Nebraska. What Trump Said About France Trump repeatedly invoked France during Monday night’s rally as he sought to frame the stakes of the November election around immigration and what he described as the future of Western countries. “If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” Trump said. Trump described France as “a once great nation” that he claimed was being “conquered, looted and burned to the ground” and blamed migrants, extremists and left-wing politicians for the country's problems. “They despise everything about France, and they’re destroying that country,” Trump said. “And we’re not going to let that happen to this country.” Trump further alleged that migrants he was referring to were refusing to assimilate into French society. “This is what’s happening to France,” Trump said. “They want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here.” Trump also recalled what he said was an earlier warning to French President Emmanuel Macron. His characterization of that conversation was not independently verified. “As I told President Macron, the president of France when I first met him many years ago, now close your border or you will lose France,” Trump said. The president broadened his criticism to other European nations, mentioning Italy and Germany and claiming that they were “losing their country.” He then tied his characterization of events in France directly to his argument against Democrats. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember, that is what the radical Democrats want to do to America,” Trump said. Trump provided no evidence that Democrats want violence or destruction in the United States. His broader argument was that Republican control of Congress was necessary to prevent the United States from experiencing the problems he attributed to immigration and left-wing policies in Europe. Protesters Interrupt Trump and Vance Trump’s speech was interrupted at least three times by protesters within its opening minutes, and some protesters were removed. Trump responded by calling them “paid protesters,” but provided no evidence for that assertion. Members of the crowd behind Trump could be seen telling one person to leave, and chanting USA. The protesters outbursts were not audible from a live feed reviewed by Newsweek. “They’re paid protesters,” Trump said, adding, “Here’s another one. Listen to that one. I can tell by the voice they get paid.” Trump later minimized the size of the protest, saying there had been “two and a half people” and predicting that news reports would characterize it as a “massive protest.” The interruptions came the same day that a protester was removed from a Vance campaign rally in Hendersonville, North Carolina. The crowd chanted “USA” as the protester was escorted from the event. The protester could be heard saying, “Release the Epstein Files. Bless our children.” Vance responded to the interruption by telling the crowd that “the American government exists for American citizens.” Republican Midterm Blitz Trump and Vance are crisscrossing the country as Republicans try to boost their candidates and drive turnout ahead of November 3. The Associated Press reported that Trump began what he called a 32-day campaign blitz at the beginning of October, traveling to Texas and Oklahoma while Vance campaigned in Florida. The appearances included heavily Republican areas where GOP candidates were facing unexpectedly difficult races. Trump has since campaigned in additional states, including Arizona and Montana. Fox News reported on October 15 that he was continuing the blitz following rallies in those states as he sought to energize Republican voters and help candidates in key races. Monday brought Trump to Kansas and Vance to North Carolina. The President is scheduled to campaign Tuesday in Greenville, North Carolina, where Spectrum News reported he is expected to boost Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley and Republican House candidate Laurie Buckhout. Trump explicitly asked supporters Monday to transfer their support for him to Republican candidates. “At this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he asked the crowd. Before the Kansas rally, Trump also argued that his campaign appearances were helping Republican candidates, saying his rallies were having a “huge impact and a positive impact on the Republican Party,” according to Fox News. State of Play for the Midterms Republicans enter the final stretch facing a difficult fight for control of Congress. In the House, Fox News’ October 13 Power Rankings forecast Democratic control, giving Democrats an advantage in at least 219 seats and Republicans an advantage in at least 198. The forecast pointed to Democrats’ generic-ballot advantage and movement in a number of individual House contests. The Senate remains closely contested. Republicans hold 53 seats, while Democrats hold 45 and two independents caucus with them. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a 51-seat majority. A 50-50 chamber would leave Vice President Vance able to cast tiebreaking votes for Republicans. Kansas has emerged as part of that battlefield. The Cook Political Report currently lists Marshall’s contest as one of seven Senate toss-ups. Cook also rates North Carolina’s open Senate contest Likely Democrat. The House battlefield includes two closely watched North Carolina contests. Cook rates both the state’s 1st District, represented by Democrat Don Davis, and its 11th District as toss-ups. Those competitive races provide the backdrop for the Republican campaign push, with Trump asking supporters in Kansas to treat November 3 as though his own name were on the ballot. news.title: From France to Albania, why protests are sweeping across Europe
news.text:
Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe.

Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries, and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs.

Young people “feel disappointed with the (social) model and experience a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” said María Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. “And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channelling that discontent and driving people into the streets.”

Cities have turned into battlefields as several top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent hybrid attacks in NATO countries.

Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction, writing on his Truth Social platform: “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” on Monday.

Many of the protests have been fuelled by frustrated young people. Other elements including black-clad, masked agitators have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants.

A look at what's driving the unrest.

Students say education resources are dwindling

In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they call understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighbourhoods.

The protests then broadened as France's CGT labour union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services.

Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend's unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds have been injured.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday's violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police.

“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address.

In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year.

Unaffordable housing stymies young people

In Madrid's central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks t o protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities.

Some things have changed since the encampment began: public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but a lack of support in Parliament meant they didn't pass, triggering a snap election announced by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez for November. A general strike will also take place in November — the first in 14 years.

Major housing protests also have taken place in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain's overtourism and housing challenges.

In Spain, the minimum wage is 1,221 euros (USD 1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around 1,130 euros (about USD 1,270), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión.

“Most of my paycheck goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do,” said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. “This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city.”

Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal's largest cities, Lisbon and Porto.

Untenable living costs as inflation rises in Italy

“Italia in Piazza,” or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, healthcare, education, and access to housing, as well as higher wages to deal with rising costs. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2 per cent in September, surpassing the eurozone's 3.8 per cent, according to government data.

The peaceful marches turned violent in three northern cities: In Turin and Bologna, and in Milan — Italy's finance and fashion capital, where rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire.

In Milan, 271 people were arrested during two days of unrest — most of them minors, police said. Fourteen members of the security forces were reportedly injured.

And now a newly formed group calling itself the “Oct. 17 Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilization,” calling supporters to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy, starting in Milan.

Students in Albania join anti-corruption protests

In Albania, anti-government protests continued Sunday for a sixth consecutive day in Tirana, featuring more clashes between demonstrators and police. The violence escalated after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.

Rama has condemned the protests, saying participants had been “ideologized and radicalized” by antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organised far-left militants in the United States, where President Donald Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organisation.

Ending corruption is a major demand of the Albanian civic movement — named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.

In Serbia, university students who have led mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are now challenging a return by the Balkan country's powerful populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in early parliamentary elections this month.

The former authoritarian president is eyeing a return as prime minister after the Oct. 25 vote. The youth-backed Students' List party is believed to be running close to Vucic's party, making the outcome uncertain and fuelling fears of possible violence.

Published on October 20, 2026
news.summary: Economic hardship, housing pressures and declining confidence in public services are drawing demonstrators onto the streets of cities across Europe.

news.text:
Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, warned the UN secretary-general and the Security Council over what the letter called the "arrogant threats" of US President Donald Trump and the Zionist regime.

In the letter to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the Security Council president, Darzi said the threats are part of US and Zionist regime wars of aggression against Iran that began on June 13, 2025 and Feb. 28, 2026, along with deliberate attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure. He said they risk further serious violations of international law with catastrophic humanitarian consequences and dangers to regional and international peace and security. He warned that responsibility rests with the United States, the Zionist regime and anyone who directly or indirectly supports their aggression and state terrorism.

The letter cited US media reports on Oct. 15, 2026 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared military options including the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iran. It said Trump discussed the weapon in a television interview the same day and threatened Iran with further attacks.

It said Israeli war minister Yisrael Katz announced on Oct. 18, 2026 that Israel was ready to attack Iran and that in any new aggression "all energy facilities" would be targeted, with the aim of returning Iran to the "Stone Age." Katz also claimed the United States and Israel had dropped 35,000 bombs on Iran in total and said their military campaign was not over.

The letter said that on the same day, the Zionist regime's prime minister, whom it described as a war criminal under international prosecution, again openly declared his criminal intent to preemptively start another war of aggression against Iran. It said the silence and explicit support of some Security Council members had made him more brazen in pursuing genocidal thinking.

The letter said the threats amount to gross violations of international law, including the threat to use the MOAB against civilian infrastructure and to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure. It said attempts to spread fear among Iran's population or any threat to deliberately destroy critical civilian infrastructure are new instances of gross violations of international humanitarian law with severe and possibly long-term humanitarian and environmental consequences, increasing the responsibility of the United States and the Zionist regime. It said both have repeatedly shown they do not consider themselves bound by any rules of international law, including obligations under the four 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law.

Iran asked the UN secretary-general and the Security Council to demand that the United States and the Zionist regime immediately end their unlawful threats and fully comply with their obligations under the UN Charter and peremptory norms of international law. It also asked them to explicitly and unambiguously condemn threats to attack Iran, including its critical civilian infrastructure, used as a tool of coercion and intimidation.

Iran further asked the Security Council to take urgent measures within its powers and duties, including holding an emergency meeting to address the threats to regional and international peace and security and to ensure accountability for the United States and the rogue Zionist regime. It asked the Council to guarantee accountability and full compensation for damages caused by wrongful international acts that the United States and the Zionist regime commit against Iran daily.

The letter said the Security Council cannot remain silent in the face of explicit threats of further aggression and destruction of critical civilian infrastructure, warning that inaction would further weaken the Charter and the international legal order on which the UN system is built.

Iran reaffirmed its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and its determination to take all necessary measures against any source of threat endangering its people, sovereignty, territorial integrity and vital national interests. It said that if the Security Council fails in its responsibilities, Iran will exercise its right of self-defense and give a decisive response in line with international law to protect its supreme national interests.

It said the United States and the Zionist regime will bear full responsibility for the consequences of any further aggression, including the risk of unpredictable and uncontrollable escalation.

Iran requested that the letter be distributed as an official document of the General Assembly and the Security Council.

news.title: Fox News Star Humiliates Trump by Detailing All His Problems
news.text:
Brit Hume has sounded the alarm on Donald Trump’s midterm sprint, and he doesn’t appear to be impressed.

Election Day is two weeks away, and Fox News’ 83-year-old senior political analyst used his Monday appearance on Special Report with Bret Baier to list the mounting problems facing the 80-year-old president’s haphazard attempt to save the GOP from tanking in the midterms. 

Hume’s got the numbers on his side. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday found Trump’s approval rating has sunk to 31 percent, a new low for his political career, with Democrats holding a 12-point edge on the generic congressional ballot. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey conducted Oct. 9–13 and published Sunday put his approval at 33 percent.

“The president has been out campaigning vigorously, but I’m not sure it’s making any difference, and what difference it makes, I’m not sure is helping,” Hume said, in his trademark deadpan. 

Exhibit A: Texas.

“He’s calling James Talarico, ‘Tala-freak-o,’” Hume told Baier, 56.

Talarico is a former teacher and Austin-area state lawmaker. Facing off against Trump-endorsed Republican nominee Ken Paxton, he is a rising star Democrat and a proud progressive populist. Both are vying for the Senate seat vacated by Sen. John Cornyn, whom Paxton ousted in May. A Fox 7 survey shows a tight contest, with Talarico holding a wafer-thin lead. Trump has explained the nickname by claiming Talarico is “a little freaky.”

Hume said, “Now look, it’s true that James Talarico has endorsed some pretty exotic positions in his years in public life, and that he is not on paper, at least, a very good fit for the state of Texas. However, what he does not seem to be is a freak.”

“You see him, he seems mild-mannered, he seems pleasant, he’s not an unattractive candidate, whether you agree with him or not,” he added.

Hume then turned to foreign policy, saying, “This cuddling up to Vladimir Putin at this moment, and his turning his back seemingly once again on Volodymyr Zelensky, I don’t think that plays well.” 

Late Friday night, Trump suspended a sweeping package of Russia sanctions that Congress passed just last month. This drew fire from both parties. It came days after he agreed to buy Russian diesel to bring down fuel prices, which have soared since he went to war with Iran.

Trump turned on Zelensky over the weekend, claiming the Ukrainian leader “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” before telling reporters Monday he’d be open to peace talks with Putin and Xi Jinping without Zelensky at the table.

“The American public isn’t really sold on Zelensky, but it favors him... by some margin,” Hume said. “They can’t stand Putin. I mean, the polling on Putin is just terrible.”

He also pointed to the White House’s press secretary debacle, calling it a “fiasco.”

“They sent the poor person out there with no time to prepare, really, only a matter of a day or two, and it didn’t go well,” Hume said. “Well, of course it didn’t. It was crazy to send her out like that.”

Hume didn’t name her, but he was referring to Katie Zacharia, who left the role on Oct. 16 after less than a week in the job. Her exit is the shortest tenure of any U.S. press secretary on record. 

Zacharia had blamed her disastrous debut briefing on having “very little prep time,” telling Fox News’ Sean Hannity, “I received briefing materials in the morning.”

Hume concluded, “So I don’t see this White House and this campaigning by the president as having made much headway so far,” Hume concluded.

Host Baier then turned to the riots engulfing France, where student protests over school conditions have spiraled into the country’s worst unrest in years, CNN reported. 

Hume said the chaos “might change the political atmosphere” if it reached American soil, but added: “If it doesn’t spread here... I’m not sure how much of an effect it will have on this election.”

The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment.

news.title: Oil eases as markets assess potential waiver on Russian energy, Middle East supply risks
news.text:
Oil prices fell on Tuesday as markets ​weighed an executive order from US President Donald Trump that waived some sanctions and ‌tariffs tied to Russian energy exports, while attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen kept fears of Middle East supply disruptions in view.

Brent crude futures fell 49 cents, or 0.45%, to $109.06 a barrel by 0010 GMT. ​

The US West Texas Intermediate crude (WTI) contract for November delivery , set to expire on ​Tuesday, eased 0.33% to $103.32.

The more-active December contract was down 46 cents, or ⁠0.47%, at $98.08.

Brent rose as high as $110.70 per barrel in the previous session, its highest ​since May 20.

An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related US sanctions and ​tariffs, including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas.

However, Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio ​said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.

Russia’s crude oil production increased by 65,000 barrels ​per day in September to 8.43 million bpd, but remained some 870,000 bpd below a year ago, the International Energy ‌Agency ⁠said last week.

“While the prospect of additional Russian diesel supply offers some theoretical relief, traders appear far more focused on the ongoing risk of further damage to energy infrastructure across the Gulf region,” Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said.

Yemen’s Houthis said on Monday they carried ​out several attacks against Saudi ​energy, airport and military ⁠targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport. Saudi authorities did not ​immediately confirm the claims and Reuters could not independently verify them.

Meanwhile, 58 ​people were ⁠killed and more than 200 were injured after an attack on Monday by the Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province.

The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and ⁠underscored ​continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping ​oil prices above $100 a barrel.

In the US, crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product ​inventories, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Monday.

news.text:
He told US senators on Monday that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” even though they had already been paid for by Ukraine’s European allies. 

The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place.

The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles, with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine. 

He also said that Ukraine’s European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US . 

 ”The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “But unfortunately, there is still no approval.”

Earlier on Monday, he said Ukraine had again not received any early warnings about incoming Russian missile strikes. The country is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia. 

There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data.

The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions.

The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings, cutting off electricity to more than half a million households.

“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack. 

The US, though, dismissed claims it was withholding information, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisting that Washington had not paused its intelligence sharing with Kyiv. 

Regarding the easing of sanctions and the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow, Donald Trump strongly criticized Zelenskyy for calling out the deal.

news.title: Zelensky lobbies US senators to pressure Trump – Axios
news.text:
Vladimir Zelensky has appealed to a bipartisan group of US senators to pressure President Donald Trump into lifting alleged restrictions on American military assistance and intelligence sharing, Axios reported on Monday.

During a virtual meeting with lawmakers led by Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democrat Richard Blumenthal on Monday, Zelensky complained about alleged disruptions to weapons deliveries, satellite communications and early warnings of Russian missile attacks, according to a transcript obtained by Axios from Ukrainian officials.

The Ukrainian leader suggested that Washington had deliberately “slowed down support” to force Kiev into accepting a negotiated settlement with Moscow.

The lobbying effort comes as Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Kiev’s refusal to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which the American president has blamed for worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for US consumers.

The dispute escalated earlier this month after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and increase supplies to the global market. Kiev publicly condemned the agreement, accusing Washington of making concessions to Moscow behind Ukraine’s back.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly reminded Ukrainian negotiators during talks in Miami that Washington was supplying Kiev with weapons and intelligence and that Ukraine should not pursue attacks that hurt American consumers. Ukrainian officials interpreted the remarks as a threat to suspend that assistance unless the refinery strikes stopped.

Washington has denied issuing any such ultimatum. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected claims that Washington deliberately restricted intelligence sharing or Starlink access. The Pentagon has likewise denied changing its intelligence-sharing policy.

Yet Zelensky continued to challenge the administration, telling senators that SpaceX’s Starlink and the US military’s Starshield satellite systems remained partially restricted and that Ukraine had missed US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile attacks on three occasions over the past week.

He also accused Secretary of War Pete Hegseth of holding up Patriot interceptor missiles and AIM-9X missiles that NATO countries had already purchased for Kiev. The Washington Post separately reported that the Pentagon had yet to authorize certain transfers of Patriot missiles from third countries.

Following the meeting, Blumenthal pledged further congressional action, saying bipartisan support for Kiev remained “clear and unequivocal.”

Trump, meanwhile, lashed out at Zelensky on Monday, accusing him of obstructing efforts to end the conflict and suggesting that someone else should negotiate on Ukraine’s behalf.

“Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump told reporters. “Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get someone else to negotiate… We’ve given a lot to Ukraine, they’ve given nothing to us.”

The Ukrainian leader has sought congressional intervention amid an increasingly bitter confrontation with the White House
