news.title: Trump seeks nuclear talks with China, Russia
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 20 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has expressed willingness to hold a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss nuclear arms reductions, potentially during his planned visit to China next month, as Washington seeks to revive arms-control diplomacy among the world's three major nuclear powers. Speaking to reporters before departing the White House on Monday, Trump indicated that he was open to a proposed trilateral meeting but wanted nuclear weapons and denuclearisation to be central to the discussions rather than Russia's continuing war in Ukraine. "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, we would have it to talk about denuclearization," Trump said. The President's comments followed reports that Putin had proposed a meeting involving the leaders of Russia, China and the United States during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November. No formal agreement to hold such a summit has been announced, and the three governments have not confirmed a common agenda or timetable for nuclear negotiations. Trump said he was prepared to discuss reducing nuclear weapons with both Moscow and Beijing, describing such negotiations as an opportunity to address one of the world's most serious security challenges. The President has repeatedly expressed interest in a nuclear agreement involving the three countries, although their strategic arsenals differ substantially in size and composition. The United States and Russia possess the world's largest nuclear stockpiles, while China has been expanding its nuclear capabilities. Trump said China remained behind the two other powers but was increasing its capabilities. His latest remarks came days after he said in an October 15 interview that Washington was already discussing denuclearisation with Russia and China. The President acknowledged that reaching an agreement would be difficult, particularly because Beijing possesses a smaller arsenal and may be reluctant to accept the same limitations as Washington and Moscow. China has previously opposed proposals for trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations on the grounds that its arsenal is substantially smaller than those of the United States and Russia. The Chinese Foreign Ministry reiterated that position last week, saying that expecting Beijing to participate in three-way nuclear disarmament talks at the present stage was neither fair nor realistic. The possibility of renewed negotiations comes amid growing uncertainty over international nuclear arms-control arrangements. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, commonly known as New START, expired earlier this year, leaving Washington and Moscow without the legally binding strategic nuclear limits established under the agreement. The treaty had limited each country to 1,550 deployed strategic nuclear warheads and imposed restrictions on deployed delivery systems. Arms-control specialists have warned that the absence of a successor agreement could accelerate competition among nuclear powers and weaken transparency over strategic arsenals. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said on Monday that meaningful negotiations would require detailed proposals and sustained diplomatic engagement. Russia has suggested that a meeting involving Trump and Xi could address the conflict, while Ukrainian officials have expressed concern about discussions affecting their country's future without Kyiv's participation. Trump's remarks indicated that he would prefer to place nuclear arms control at the centre of any three-way meeting.

news.title: ‘Trump Has Been Putin’s Puppet’ – US Congresswoman Slams White House Over Ukraine Aid Delays
news.text:
Democratic Congresswoman Madeleine Dean accused US President Donald Trump of acting as Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “puppet,” calling his administration’s treatment of Ukraine “historically dishonorable” after President Volodymyr Zelensky briefed a bipartisan group of American lawmakers on delayed weapons deliveries and disruptions to crucial battlefield intelligence.

Speaking in an interview with MS NOW’s Peter Alexander on Monday, Oct. 19, shortly after participating in the call with Zelensky, Dean said the Ukrainian president had described mounting difficulties defending his country against Russian attacks despite Ukrainian forces making battlefield gains.

“I find it historically dishonorable that this administration has engaged in a series of consequences that really support Putin and harm Ukraine,” the Pennsylvania Democrat said.

Dean pointed to Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia, a controversial Russian diesel supply agreement, restrictions affecting US-supported satellite communications, and delays in delivering weapons already paid for by European allies.

Dean rejected the prospect of Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping discussing Ukraine’s future without Kyiv’s participation.

“We need real diplomats,” Dean said. “This war should have been ended long ago if the US played the indispensable nation that it should be.”

“But instead, we have found that our president, and this is sad, he has been a puppet of Putin.”

$400 Million in Weapons Held Up, Dean Says

Dean said Zelensky had informed lawmakers that approximately $400 million worth of weapons intended for Ukraine had not been released because US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had yet to authorize their delivery.

She said Kyiv had repeatedly contacted the Trump administration, including Hegseth, seeking approval but received no response.

“$400 million – this is what President Zelensky said – in weapons not coming and not released, Mr. Hegseth failing to sign for their release,” Dean said.

The congresswoman also raised concerns about restrictions affecting Starlink and Starshield, the satellite communications services developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

According to Dean, a significant part of the congressional conversation focused on the consequences of reduced satellite capabilities and interruptions in early warnings of Russian missile attacks.

The congresswoman warned that the disruptions had deadly consequences, undermining Ukraine’s ability to detect incoming Russian strikes and protect civilians.

The Trump administration has denied deliberately restricting intelligence-sharing with Kyiv.

‘Is It Just to Force Ukraine to the Table?’

Dean said lawmakers had directly questioned whether the administration’s actions were intended to force Zelensky into accepting a peace agreement favorable to Moscow.

“Is it just to force Ukraine to a table, that they will lose so much that they will continue to suffer bloodshed and no warnings of attacks as we hit another difficult winter?” she asked, recalling the discussion.

“Is it just to push him to a table and to accede to whatever Mr. Putin wants?”

According to Dean, Zelensky did not claim to know Trump’s intentions.

“Mr. Zelensky was honest. He said, I don’t really know the motivation of the president, of our president,” she recalled.

Dean, however, offered her own assessment.

“I find it historically dishonorable that the president has turned and showed his cards, that he supports Mr. Putin in this effort, the one who is bloodthirsty and has cost tens of thousands of lives.”

Her remarks came as Trump defended his recent Russian diesel agreement and again criticized Zelensky, saying it was time for “somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”

‘Nothing About Ukraine Without Ukraine’

Dean also strongly rejected reports that Trump, Putin and Xi could meet in China next month to discuss a settlement to Russia’s war against Ukraine without Kyiv’s participation.

“Absurd,” she responded when asked about the proposal, which the interviewer compared to a new Yalta summit.

“It did come up on the call, of course, and of course the refrain is nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” she said.

Dean questioned the prospect of the leaders of the US, Russia and China deciding Ukraine’s future without its elected government.

“That Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin and our administration would decide the fate of the democracy, the young democracy, the courageous people of Ukraine and their sovereignty? Insane.”

The remarks followed reports that Putin was seeking a three-way meeting with Trump and Xi during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned Monday that such a meeting would “only encourage Putin to continue this war.”

Bipartisan Lawmakers Alarmed Over Ukraine Policy

Dean emphasized that Monday’s meeting with Zelensky included Republicans and Democrats from both chambers of Congress, including Senators Richard Blumenthal and Thom Tillis and Representative Gregory Meeks.

She said the lawmakers who participated were strongly supportive of Ukraine and understood the consequences of reduced American assistance.

“My hope is that the Republicans, particularly members of the Senate, who are close with this president, will offer their outrage, and more importantly, their demand that we support Ukraine,” she said.

Dean also called on Republicans to insist that Ukraine be included in any negotiations concerning an end to the war.

In a joint statement following the meeting, Blumenthal and Tillis confirmed that Zelensky had raised concerns about degraded satellite services, interruptions in early-warning intelligence and delays in critical air defense interceptors.

“Funding Russia’s war machine, disabling Ukraine’s satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace,” the senators said.

They warned that efforts to appease Putin would prolong the war and increase casualties, reaffirming bipartisan congressional support for Ukraine.

Separately, Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen accused the administration of providing Moscow with a financial lifeline through the Russian diesel agreement and sanctions relief.

Dean’s comments came as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. On Monday, a Russian drone struck a public park in the Kharkiv region, killing six civilians, including two children.
news.summary: S Congresswoman Madeleine Dean accused Trump of helping Putin by delaying $400 million in weapons for Ukraine, disrupting missile warnings and easing sanctions on Russia.

But Trump still retains the power to block most major legislation.- With a bigger majority, voters likely will look to Democrats to address their economic concerns, not just oppose Trump.- Trump gains a political foil, allowing him to share blame for Washington's shortcomings and potentially pin economic problems and high prices on Democrats, who he can say are now co-responsible for the economy.Senate Democratic majority: 8 seats or more- Democrats could claim a clear electoral mandate and argue that voters rebuked Trump's handling of the first half of his second term.- Democrats enter fiscal negotiations with Republicans and the White House over government funding and the debt ceiling from their strongest position, because they have more votes to pass the relevant bills.- Democrats still lack the votes to overcome filibusters, override vetoes or convict Trump in any impeachment trial if House Democrats decide to impeach him.Impact: Democrats gain greater leverage but governing remains constrained by Trump's veto, the filibuster and shared political responsibility for the economy.REPUBLICANS KEEP CONTROL OF BOTH HOUSE AND SENATEWhile unlikely, given the number of vulnerable House Republicans defending seats, this remains possible.Impact: Trump and Republicans would claim a fresh mandate for his final two years in office. news.title: Trump signs order to boost women's health
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 20 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order directing the establishment of a dedicated women's health division within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House task force to accelerate research into diseases affecting women, with Indian-American NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya among the senior officials attending the announcement. The initiative, unveiled at a White House ceremony on Monday alongside First Lady Melania Trump, seeks to expand research into women's health, encourage the use of advanced technologies and improve access to medical treatments. The executive order, "Advancing Women's Health to Improve Outcomes in All Phases of Life", establishes a White House Women's Health Task Force to coordinate efforts across federal agencies. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the task force, which held its first meeting later Monday. Trump said the initiative would address diseases and medical conditions affecting women that have historically received insufficient research attention. "Despite amazing advances in medical science, many diseases and conditions that disproportionately affect women remain chronically understudied," Trump said. He said the new division would promote research into these conditions and encourage the development of technologies for earlier diagnosis and improved treatment. "The executive order I'll sign in just a moment will direct the Department of Health and Human Services to establish a new women's health division within the National Institute of Health," Trump said. The President credited Melania Trump with developing the initiative and said the administration would support efforts to improve healthcare for women and girls. The First Lady outlined five priorities for the programme, beginning with directing research funding towards diseases that uniquely affect women. She also called for using advanced artificial intelligence to improve understanding of female biology and accelerate medical discoveries. Her other priorities included speeding the transition of promising therapies from laboratories to patients while maintaining safety standards, making medical advances affordable and encouraging more open discussion of women's health issues. "Beginning today, we will change the reality of women's health," Melania Trump said. She described the initiative as an opportunity to use emerging scientific capabilities, including advanced biotechnology and artificial intelligence, to address longstanding gaps in medical research. The First Lady said the programme should serve women throughout their lives, from childhood and motherhood to later years. "Start by directing research funding towards finding cures for diseases that affect women in a unique way," she said. She also emphasised that medical advances should be accessible to women regardless of their financial circumstances. Among those attending the ceremony were NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, Second Lady Usha Vance, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, and senior administration officials. Trump acknowledged Bhattacharya during his remarks and thanked him for his work at the NIH. The President also welcomed Usha Vance, who attended the ceremony with her infant child. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was recognised during the event, with Trump referring to her recovery from breast cancer. The announcement coincided with Breast Cancer Awareness Month, observed annually in October. The National Institutes of Health is the principal biomedical research agency of the United States, supporting scientific studies into diseases, treatments and public health. Its research programmes include work on conditions affecting women, reproductive health and sex-related differences in disease.

news.title: Oil-rich Alberta votes on Canada breakup
news.text:
EDMONTON, (Canada): Canada’s province of Alberta votes Monday on whether to hold a binding referendum on splitting from the country, with Prime Minister Mark Carney warning a separatist win would trigger crippling uncertainty during a crisis in US relations.

Polls indicate less than a quarter of people in the western Canadian province support independence.

But attention has focused on turnout in the days before the vote, and whether a motivated separatist camp could defy the polls, helped by complacency on the federalist side.

“Canada is worth fighting for,” Carney said Monday in a post on X, days after he warned people that “turnout will determine the outcome” of the vote.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has called the referendum “a dangerous bluff” as US President Donald Trump wages a trade war and levels annexation threats aimed — the prime minister says — at breaking Canadian resolve.

Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves and the province’s independence push has drawn sustained interest from Trump allies.

Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and a top Trump supporter, posted on X this month Alberta “should separate.” Separatist leaders have also held meetings at the US State Department and met with Republican political operatives.

Oil grievances Much of Alberta’s separatist momentum has been driven by anger over Ottawa’s management of the energy sector.

Many Albertans loathed Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who they accused of trying to suppress oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.

“If you want me to pinpoint who is responsible for the separatist sentiment, I think it’s Justin Trudeau,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told the Canadaland podcast this month.

At a separatist rally in Edmonton on Saturday, 61-year-old Sandy Martel said people connected to the oil industry feel “robbed, cheated (and) mistreated.”

“It’s time to stand up and say stop,” she told AFP.

The vote comes days after a fire at a military base in the province left at least four soldiers dead and wounded dozens, prompting a national outpouring of condolences.

‘Huge uncertainty’

Smith, a conservative, says she wants Alberta to remain in Canada but called the referendum to settle the divisive issue.

If a majority votes to separate, she has pledged to move forward with a binding referendum.

If the federalists win, Smith says the secession question should be considered closed.

Analysts have compared Smith’s tactics to those of former UK prime minister David Cameron, who had hoped to resolve the debate over Britain’s European Union membership with a vote.

Carney led the Bank of England through the turmoil that surrounded Brexit, and issued a warning to Albertans about that experience on Thursday.

“It wasn’t clear what ‘Brexit’ meant at the time,” he told a Calgary television station.

“For the next few years, while that was being determined, there was huge uncertainty, investments stopped, the economy started to underperform,” he added, cautioning over unintended economic consequences.

AI influence

Monday’s referendum features 10 questions, including several related to immigration, but top focus is on question 10, which asks voters to choose between: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada?” or should the province launch the process for a binding referendum on “whether or not Alberta should separate.”

Alberta’s election authority says ballots for question 10 will be counted first, with results expected in the early hours Tuesday.

Polls are open from 9:00 am (1500 GMT) to 8:00 pm.

Elections Alberta says 3.1 million are eligible to vote, with 1.4 million people having already cast advanced or special ballots as of Sunday.

news.title: Florida Issues Arrest Warrant for Former Cuban Leader Raúl Castro
news.text:
Florida is seeking to arrest former Cuban leader Raúl Castro over his alleged role in a conspiracy to shoot down and murder three U.S. citizens and one lawful resident aboard two civilian aircraft more than 30 years ago.

The state arrest warrant was announced Monday by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who accused Castro of having spies embedded in America to help carry out the shooting down of two unarmed planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a humanitarian organization that promotes Cubans’ efforts against the country’s long-standing communist regime.

“Raúl Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier said in a news release. “The Castro regime’s spies operated in our communities, fed intelligence to Havana, and helped put civilian pilots in the crosshairs of Cuban MiGs.”

The four victims in the planes shot down on Feb. 24, 1996, were Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr.

According to the affidavit, Castro, who was the minister of Cuba’s Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president at the time of the incident, was the final decider in authorizing the attack, giving senior military officials an order to “shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone.”

Cuban spies operating in South Florida’s Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties infiltrated the Brothers to the Rescue organization and reported their flight plans back to Cuban leaders, the news release said.

On the day of the attack, three unarmed Brothers to the Rescue aircraft departed the Opa-Locka Airport in Miami-Dade County. Once they crossed the 24th latitude line, while still outside the island-nation’s territory, Cuban MiGs destroyed two of the civilian Cessnas with missiles, killing the four onboard.

“For thirty years, their families and our Cuban American community have carried this profound loss and refused to let the pursuit of justice fade,” Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said in the news release. “Today’s action sends a clear message: the passage of time does not diminish the value of these lives or our responsibility to pursue accountability.”

The news release added that the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba and received no warning before the attack.

Elements of the alleged criminal conspiracy, like the gathering of intel by stateside Cuban spies, occurred in Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties. Chief Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan of the 11th Judicial Circuit, which encompasses Miami-Dade, signed the arrest warrant.

Florida’s Office of Statewide Prosecution has assumed jurisdiction of the ongoing investigation, Uthmeier said, and additional charges against Castro are possible.

“Under President [Donald] Trump’s administration, we’re committed to pursuing every lawful, prosecutable avenue to bring accountability, including parallel federal and state prosecutions,” U.S. Attorney Jason Quiñones said in the news release.

Alina Fernández Revuelta, the daughter of Fidel Castro, welcomed the charges against her uncle.

“The charges increase pressure on a regime untouchable for decades,” she told The Epoch Times in a text message. “Coming from a family directly connected to that history, you understand the weight of this moment in a different way.”
news.summary: Castro is accused of being the final decision-maker in the shooting down of two civilian aircraft more than 30 years ago.

news.title: A student who says violence is ‘legitimate’: ROBERT HARDMAN
news.text:
By ROBERT HARDMAN IN PARIS 00:28 20 Oct 2026, updated 02:33 20 Oct 2026

A picture of raw fury and utter despair, she has not merely gone viral. She has now had her face transposed online on to the Mona Lisa, Les Miserables, Joan of Arc and every other iconic image of France, her shock emblematic of an entire traumatised nation.

She is the unnamed woman filmed trying to prevent a masked mob from ransacking a Paris supermarket this weekend. ‘Arretez!’ (‘Stop’) she cries repeatedly in vain. ‘C’est pas la cause!’ (‘It’s not the cause’).

The mob push her aside contemptuously. ‘It’s feeding time!’ shouts one. ‘Grab all the wine!’ shouts another, while a terrified member of staff looks on, every bit as impotent as the French state has proved to be in recent days.

Standing outside the very same shop yesterday – a branch of the popular Franprix chain on the Rue du Faubourg du Temple – I find that the sense of shock has not subsided.

Local pensioner Annie Tyger arrives, clutching a couple of shopping bags, and finds boards across the windows. Sheets of cracked, reinforced glass lie in heaps on the pavement. A security guard explains that there will be no shopping today (or for the rest of the week for that matter).

Annie promptly bursts into tears. ‘C’est des crapules!’ (‘They’re scum!’) she sobs. The shop manager, Kine, emerges to comfort her.

I ask if she knows the gallant woman who confronted the mob at the weekend. ‘I don’t know her name. She just comes here now and then,’ Kine tells me. ‘It was a scary moment. She was courageous.’

It certainly takes guts to stand up to a gang of masked thugs and tell them that violence is not helping their cause. But what, precisely, is that cause?

That is a question France now, disturbingly, finds itself unable to answer. This is a country with pitchforks in its DNA. The French regard protesting much as the English view cricket.

When French farmers or fishermen or pensioners or anyone else feels hard done by, they take their grievance on to the streets.

It usually does the trick, which is why their economy is a Ponzi scheme of unaffordable subsidies and everyone retires on a fat state pension at 62. Even Britain looks productive in comparison.

All this muscular civil disobedience is why France has no less than four divisions of full-time riot police (the famously no-nonsense CRS, the ‘mobile’ division of the Gendarmerie, the BRAV-M motorised rapid-response force and a more recent creation called the ‘C.I.’ or ‘intervention companies’).

They amount to more than 26,000 full-time paramilitary anti-riot personnel (in Britain we have none) who routinely deploy with an array of semi-lethal weaponry and water cannon.

Yet they proved woefully unable to contain the looting and wanton destruction which broke out across France over the weekend – a new low, even by France’s Olympian standards of rioting.

The full damage has yet to be added up but the tally of arrests has already surpassed 2,000.

And, two days later, the aggro is still simmering with more of the same to come. Traditionally, a day’s rioting is followed by relative calm. Yet I arrive in Paris on the afternoon following Saturday’s mayhem and the running battles are still going on.

Even in the early hours of yesterday morning, I find vanloads of CRS cops chasing masked gangs down one of the smartest streets in all of France, the Rue de Rivoli.

Much of it seems like a game. The police cannot match the speed of the runaways but are in jovial mood when I chat to one unit. One jokingly waves his shield which has a sticker saying ‘ACAB’ on it. This is an old English criminal acronym – ‘All Cops Are Bastards’ – yet it is a universal slogan, much beloved of rioters here in France.

It has been sprayed on walls and statues all over Paris this weekend. Yet here is a riot cop wearing it as a badge of honour.

There is still sporadic looting going on. I walk past an optician’s showroom by Rambuteau Metro station which has just been raided. Branded glasses and sunglasses are prime targets, it transpires, as they are light and easily sold on.

Further on, the police chase another hooded gang into a Metro entrance at Les Halles, the largest station on the network.

Rather than pursue them into this warren, one policeman simply lobs a tear-gas grenade down the stairs after them, and a cloud of smoke wafts back up.

There is considerable confusion between the various branches of the police. One lot wave you down a particular street; moments later another lot tell you to go the other way.

Come daylight, the situation is no clearer. Part of the reason that police control broke down over the weekend is that no one can agree on who is protesting about what.

Big student protests have been happening for several weeks, ostensibly because of poor school facilities. The students were out again all over France on Saturday, joined by the massed ranks of ‘France Unbowed’, the far-Left disciples of Jeremy Corbyn soundalike, Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is gearing up for next year’s presidential election.

Both groups share a number of grievances, not least the ‘cost-of-living crisis’ and Gaza. The same day saw a resurgence of the Gilets Jaunes movement, a working-class uprising against fuel prices and ‘austerity’ which repeatedly brought France to a standstill between 2018 and 2020.

Now it appears to have reawoken over diesel price hikes. Lumped together, all of the above amounted to what commentators have called ‘a perfect storm’ of protest this weekend.

And while Saturday’s initial marches proved to be peaceful, more sinister elements were waiting to take things further.

Starting with the occasional projectile hurled at the cops, these encounters inevitably escalated into running battles all over France.

The police used baton charges and tear gas while the rioters’ main tactic was to set fire to bins, booths and barricades.

One interesting sub-plot to these riots, incidentally, is a new tool: the burning bicycle. Ordinary bikes don’t catch fire, of course, but an e-bike can go up like a firework courtesy of its lithium battery.

All over Paris yesterday, at every e-bike collection point, I found clumps of gnarled grey cycle frames and charred wheels piled up like artefacts from Pompeii. British cops, take note.

And with the police preoccupied, of course, next came the looting. Again, this was something entirely beyond the norm – in terms of both scale and location.

It was nationwide and, in each city, it was not confined to the banlieues, the outlying troublespots populated disproportionately by ethnic minorities and the poor. Here in Paris, the looting was right in the heart of the most prosperous shopping districts.

An entire branch of Hermes lay pillaged, its trademark orange bags and boxes scattered down the street. Chanel and Christian Dior received the same treatment. A mob ran wild in Galeries Lafayette, the Parisian answer to Selfridges or Harrods. An estimated 1,500 stores across France were plundered.

Yesterday, business was brisk on clothing websites such as Vinted as customers noticed a rush of good-as-new top brands on sale in France (plenty of choice – surprise, surprise – for fans of Hermes).

Anyone tempted to scoop up a job lot of Yves Saint-Laurent nail polish at €2.54 (£2.14) a pot might first wonder whether they are likely to receive what they pay for from a brazen criminal, not to mention the ethics of buying stolen goods.

Here, though, we come across an alarming lack of basic decency – both on social media and on the streets. ‘It’s only taking from the very rich,’ is a popular sentiment.

In other words, all this amounts to victimless crime.

In the Place de la Republique, one of the capital’s main demonstration points, the famous statue of Marianne (the personification of France) is defaced from head to toe in graffiti.

The base of her pedestal has been smashed with sledgehammers to produce projectiles for throwing at the neighbouring military barracks. Two days on, no attempt has been made to remove a huge yellow vest draped over Marianne proclaiming (in French): ‘The Police Mutilate Schoolchildren.’

Here I meet Celian, 21, a fourth-year Paris University journalism student of African-Italian heritage. A calm, intelligent man, he argues that most of the weekend’s violence is acceptable.

‘The police are perpetuating physical violence against us and the wealth distribution is not fair. So, yes, this is legitimate. Whether as students or as workers, we try to talk with the government by legal and fair ways, but the government doesn’t talk or listen.’

Does that justify ransacking a shoe shop? ‘Those people who do that are just opportunists, not part of our movement. I don’t think people should invade small shops run by people with no connection to capitalism. But if people attack Starbucks or Nike, then that is a political statement because of their connection to Israel.’

He heard President Macron’s televised appeal for calm and orderly debate but he rejects it. ‘What we have learned from the Gilets Jaunes is that you must always keep moving. Never stay in the same place so the police cannot contain you. As Jean-Luc Melenchon says, we should “be like water”.’

The Left-wing leader himself has distanced himself from the thieving, saying ‘those who share our movement have no business in looting’. He fiercely rejects the government’s claims that his lot are to blame: ‘The real culprits are in government, unable to ensure both public order and the right to protest.’

All over Paris, there are two sounds: police sirens and the drills of the repair teams boarding up smashed windows. It will be months before the glaziers can replace all the glass.

The Lego store at Les Halles – France’s biggest shopping mall – is already a wall of panneaux (wooden panels). The front of Adidas and Nike are following suit when I walk by.

Another video was going viral yesterday, that of an elderly optician called Madame Ye, who moved from China to France years ago and raised a family here. She had closed early on Saturday, pulled down the shutters and gone home but, to her horror, could see marauders smashing their way in to the small shop on the Boulevard de Magenta. She rushed back.

A TikTok video captures her in shock leaving with the last tray of glasses. What it does not show is that, moments later, even these were snatched off her by masked men.

I meet her son, William, 28, a newly qualified optician, and his sisters, Vanessa and Lea. The latter is in tears as they survey the wreckage.

‘It is our only shop,’ says William. ‘All the family savings went into this. We’ve only been open a year. Our insurance won’t cover this. I don’t know what we do now.’

Family friend Zinadine Aidel, 27, is beyond furious. ‘These are the small businesses who pay the benefits of these casseurs [looters],’ he tells me.

Donald Trump has blamed this carnage on ‘immigrants’ but he is wrong. The protesters are from all faiths and backgrounds.

Most of the looters are, indeed, from ethnic minorities but they are certainly not the asylum-seeking small-boat crowd heading for Britain.

They are French-born, French-speaking French nationals: the children of second or third-generation migrants who came to build a better life here. And they are not going away.

Back in Les Halles, I meet Gabriel, manager of the Levi’s jeans store. Having wisely had his windows boarded up before Saturday’s chaos, his shop was unscathed, although it hardly looks very inviting.

When will he take the panels down? ‘Oh, not yet. We have more protests in two weeks. They will be worse.’

The same marches are now scheduled all over again for the end of the month.

news.title: As midterms loom, Trump seizes on France unrest for political gain
news.text:
APAs midterms loom, Trump seizes on France unrest for political gain

Washington: US President Donald Trump used the protests roiling France to score some quick political points Monday, as the upcoming midterm elections force his Republican party to face strong headwinds.While speaking with reporters Trump recalled an exchange with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron: "I told him a long time ago, you're making a big mistake in France. You're letting everybody from the world come in...Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon."Earlier Monday, the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"Cost-of-living demonstrations broke out across France over the weekend, with many devolving into looting and violent conflict, prompting officials to institute partial curfews Monday.While the French protests were inspired by soaring inflation, Trump has molded the violent clashes with police into evidence in favor of the anti-immigration policies he used to successfully campaign for reelection in 2024.Live Events"They're taking this French crisis and turning it into a campaign argument," JC Lintzenich, a senior fellow with the German Marshall Fund think tank, told AFP.Conservative talking pointsOpinion polls heavily favor Trump's rival Democratic Party in the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine who will take control of Congress.With just two weeks to go before Americans go to the polls, Trump has grasped any strategy he can to compel voters to support the Republican party and his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement."Since the beginning of the MAGA movement, Europe has been an extension of the US political battlefield, so it's not surprising that when there are events like the unrest from October 17, the political machine gets moving," Justin Vaisse, a professor of US foreign policy at Johns Hopkins University, told AFP.As videos of France's unrest began surfacing on social media, Trump's Vice President JD Vance wrote Saturday on X: "Western liberals imported the third world into France...they ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility."Right-wing US media personalities, including Glenn Beck, Benny Johnson, Nick Sortor and Jack Posobiec made similar points, blaming immigrants from Muslim-majority countries for causing a crisis in Western identity."The riots are viewed as validation of the warnings against immigration in general and Muslim immigration, if such a thing exists," Vaisse said.Celia Belin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations and head of its Paris office, views the commentary as an "export of domestic policies" from a US administration that openly supports nationalist parties in Europe.She told AFP that Trump and his allies "rushed into this argument, the same one that Vance had presented in Munich" in 2025, in a controversial speech described as a US culture war against Europe, with the goal of "fanning the flames."Polling prioritiesExperts note that this rhetorical strategy, while it may have succeeded in 2024, is not necessarily what US voters want to hear these days."When you look at the campaign ads here -- I'm in South Carolina right now -- it's about healthcare, domestic issues," Lintzenich said."The international element is a blip on the radar, and Ukraine, and Iran, and other ongoing national security issues rate higher than the current French instability," he continued.A Pew Research poll this month found the economy plays an important role in the choice of 82 percent of US voters, a far higher number than immigration (59 percent) or race-related issues (36 percent).Though Trump has followed through on his 2024 campaign promise to crack down on immigration, he has fared less successfully on his other promise to tamp down on inflation, with his tariff policies and war with Iran spiking prices across the economy, plunging his approval rating to record lows.Vaisse said using linking US identitarian rhetoric with the events in France "is not going to win a single vote" for Republicans, though it could "mobilize the base" to vote.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source news.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine got no early warning from partners as Russia hits the power grid again
news.text: Russia launched new attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, adding that Kyiv again received no early warning of the attack from partner countries that previously shared their intelligence.Zelenskyy is grappling with recent Washington moves benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin, including waiving U.S. sanctions on Moscow and signing a deal to import diesel from Moscow.Moscow and Kyiv, meanwhile, were discussing the possible evacuation of the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region, where about 2,000 people have been cut off from food and medical supplies for months, according to a Ukrainian human rights official.WATCH: 'I'm not looking to break up negotiations right in the middle': Trump on Russia's ongoing talks with UkraineVital US supplies are running late, Zelenskyy saysZelenskyy said speed restrictions are still in place on Kyiv’s use of the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s satellite internet service.Full service was being restored at the end of last week, but Zelenskyy said Monday that the restrictions are still slowing Ukraine's drones along the front.Also, a severe shortage of American-made Patriot air defense systems has made Ukraine more vulnerable. Delays are still occurring with some “vital supplies” from the U.S., Zelenskyy said without elaborating, and senior Kyiv officials are urgently contacting other countries to strengthen air defenses.Western intelligence sharing has helped Ukraine counter Russia’s devastating ballistic missiles and hold back Moscow’s full-scale invasion, which began more than 4½ years ago.U.S. President Donald Trump says Washington hasn’t stopped providing intelligence to Kyiv. Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeated that position Monday, saying he had no information about the previous night’s Russian attack.RELATED NEWS | Ukraine's new drone is built to airlift injured soldiers to safety when every second countsRussian barrage kills a 21-year-old womanThe Russian nighttime barrage hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than a half-million people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media.Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and its surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, with officials in the capital reporting a 21-year-old woman was killed.Ukraine received no warning from its partners ahead of the first wave of attacks, and information about a second wave arrived too late for air raid sirens to be activated in time, air force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on national television.The Russian Defense Ministry said that it struck Ukrainian targets including a data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, an industrial facility making drone components, and a locomotive depot where missiles are stored.It also said it struck a bulk carrier in the Black Sea heading for Odesa with supplies for Ukraine’s armed forces.MORE FROM UKRAINE | Ukraine defies Trump and launches one of its biggest drone attacks on Russia this yearUkraine says it has made every diplomatic effort for peaceTrump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting the war with Russia to end. Washington's efforts to bring peace, meanwhile, have failed, including a recent truce covering energy infrastructure that Trump had demanded.Help from Western allies has been vital for Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s bigger military, but fears have mounted that Trump may be turning his back on Ukraine.Western analysts and officials say Putin believes that he can wait for foreign support for Ukraine to unravel and that Russia’s bigger military will then crush Ukraine’s resistance.“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end. We have responded positively to EVERY ceasefire proposal,” Zelenskyy said Monday on social media. “The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia’s desire to drag this war out.”Ukraine has held back Moscow's forces on the front line and has hit back with long-range strikes on oil refineries deep inside Russia that triggered fuel shortages.On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St. Petersburg.Some Kyiv residents shrug, but others express growing alarmRussia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping malls, gas stations and supermarkets, among other sites.Kyiv resident Serhii Brezhniuk, owner of a shopping mall store damaged Monday, said he had grown used to the relentless bombardment.“It’s what we see every single day,” he told The Associated Press. “We’ve grown accustomed to it.”Alla Suska, 66, said she noticed many people walking around with bags under their eyes from a lack of sleep.“Since there are attacks every night and air raid alerts all day long, naturally, we don’t get any proper rest,” she said.Maksym Maksymovych, 44, said he felt the tension mounting amid Russia's escalation. His son's school was damaged in the attack, he said.“You sort of get used to all these events — after all, we’ve been living in Kyiv since the war began — but you can see the explosions drawing closer and closer,” he said.Suffering front-line city gets attentionRussia and Ukraine are engaged in talks on ending the plight of people trapped in Oleshky, Ukrainian human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said in an interview with Espreso.Oleshky has gotten global attention in recent weeks as the desperate plight of its trapped civilians came to light. There is no electricity, heat or running water in the city, which was seized by Russia on the first day of the 2022 invasion, and escaping it is fraught with risk from mined roads and drone attacks. It sits across the Dnipro River from Kherson, which is held by Ukrainian troops.Both sides blame each other for bringing the city to the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe. Russia says Ukraine deliberately blocks supplies and evacuations; Kyiv counters that Moscow is effectively holding civilians hostage.Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone Friday with Putin and urged a ceasefire to allow aid into Oleshky and to safely evacuate civilians. The Kremlin said Putin voiced support for Vatican efforts to help protect the population and secure vital supplies, and voiced readiness to cooperate. Leo spoke Monday to Zelenskyy and urged cooperation with Russia on Oleshky, the Vatican said.Possible US-China-Russia talks on the war rejected by KyivU.S. and Russian officials said Monday that talks are continuing on the possibility of a trilateral meeting involving Putin, Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at an APEC summit in China next month to try to negotiate a deal on Ukraine, without Kyiv’s participation. The possibility was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.Rubio said he was aware of the possibility. “I mean, I think there’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know if anything’s been finalized,” he told reporters.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that while the prospect of such a meeting has been mentioned, “no substantive proposals or agreements neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content have been discussed or put forward by anyone.”Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha dismissed the idea of peace talks without Kyiv, saying it would embolden Putin.“Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve," Sybiha said on X.Lithuania bolsters security after Starlink base arson attemptLithuania raised alert levels at more than 15 strategic infrastructure sites after an arson attempt Sunday at a Starlink base station in Vilnius, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday.European officials and law enforcement have warned repeatedly that Russia is waging a hybrid war against Europe, including sabotage, arson and vandalism, as well as influence operations.
news.summary: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Kyiv received no early warning of new Russian attacks from partner countries that previously shared their intelligence.

news.title: World News | Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangho Condemns Closure, Commercial Conversion Attempt of Historic Ramlila Temple in Pakistan
news.text:
Dhaka [Bangladesh], October 20 (ANI): Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangho expresses deep concern, strong condemnation and vigorous protest over the incident of sealing and closing down the centuries-old, historic "Ramlila Temple" located in Dera Ismail Khan of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, Pakistan. 

On Saturday, when news regarding the closure of Pakistan's historic Ramlila Temple and attempts to construct a commercial building spread through the media, Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangho voiced its severe condemnation, protest and resentment against this action.

"Our organisation, which firmly believes in the non-communal spirit of the great Liberation War, equality, and the core mantra of religious freedom, considers any attempt to destroy or force the closure of a place of worship to be a grave violation of basic human rights and freedom of religion", Bangladesh Hindu Sammilon Sangha said in a statement.

According to media reports, the evil plot to demolish the historic Ramlila Temple and construct a commercial building on its site is deeply tragic and contrary to global communal harmony.

"We extend our solidarity and full support to the brave resistance mounted by the local Hindu community and members of civil society against this attempt to destroy the historic structure", it added. "We call upon the Government of Pakistan to immediately ensure the security of this historic and traditional temple, permanently halt all attempts to build a commercial complex, and restore the right to conduct religious practices and rituals at the location. At the same time, we demand exemplary punishment for those identified behind this heinous incident", the statement said.

"We also humbly request the international community to raise a stronger voice to protect minority rights and religious freedom in every corner of the world", it said.

Earlier on Sunday, authorities in Pakistan’s Dera Ismail Khan sealed the historic Ram Leela Temple in Rahim Bazaar, raising concerns over the protection of religious heritage and the conversion of a culturally significant site into a commercial property.

The move came days after civil society activists intervened to prevent the demolition of the building for the construction of a commercial plaza, as reported by Dawn.

According to Dawn, the temple had previously been sealed by Assistant Commissioner Hamid Siddiq following public protests, with construction activities halted at the site.

The latest sealing has renewed concerns among residents and heritage advocates over the future of the historic structure. The development coincided with a joint meeting of civil society representatives and members of the Hindu community to discuss the reported demolition plans. Participants strongly opposed the proposed commercial construction and urged elected representatives to raise the issue in Pakistan’s National Assembly. (ANI)

news.title: Elissa Slotkin calls backlash to threat of prosecution comments 'manufactured outrage'
news.text: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., called the backlash against her comments that the threat of prosecution could deter young people from working for the Trump administration "manufactured outrage" during television interviews Monday. During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, Slotkin drew criticism after a clip went viral showing her saying she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump and push a "deterrence message" for young people. "I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.’ I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that,’" she said. "I want that deterrence message," Slotkin said. While speaking with CNN's Jake Tapper on Monday, Slotkin responded to a comment from Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, who wrote that it was "absolutely disgraceful" to "threaten young Americans for participating in politics and serving their country" with legal retribution. MIKE DAVIS: SEN SLOTKIN REVEALS HER INSIDIOUS SCHEME TO TARGET YOUNG CONSERVATIVES "Yeah, well, look, that’s manufactured outrage," Slotkin responded. "That’s his specialty. I think the thing that I’ve heard from my own Republican colleagues and peers, including interns and folks who work around the Hill who come to our events, they’ll tell you, 'I was worried. My parents were worried, you know. It’s really messy. I’m not sure what to get involved in.' Politics, in general, has become messy." "But, you know, when you’re being forced by this administration, for instance, to sign a contract that is given over to a company that Trump Jr. is on the board of, and you know that that’s a problem," she added. Slotkin then referenced her viral video from 2025, in which she and five other Democratic lawmakers urged military members to "refuse illegal orders." She claimed that in both circumstances she was only encouraging people to reject illegal activity. "My point is, do not get yourself involved in illegal activity," she said. "It’s the same thing I was talking about a year ago. Whether you’re the uniformed military or a civilian in government, if you’re being asked to do something by the president or his team, that’s illegal, you have a responsibility to reject that. That is my point, and that was the point I was trying to make." SLOTKIN SAYS DEMOCRATIC PARTY NEEDS 'NEW LEADERSHIP': 'OLD MODELS ARE NO LONGER WORKING' Fox News Digital reached out to Lee's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's previous comments on Slotkin. "That's a hell of a statement. Slotkin said that there should be prosecutions in order to scare people from going into politics. That's a Democrat and that's what they do. That's all they're good at — and you know what? That's why they're getting their a--es kicked," Trump said. Slotkin reiterated that she had no intention of targeting people for prosecution solely because of their political affiliation and only cared about people "breaking the law." "If you are violating the law, then you should be held accountable, and that includes people who are supporting that activity. That’s the point I was trying to make. You’re not breaking the law? No problem. We can have disagreements all day long, and certainly Democrats and Republicans do. I don’t care if it’s just freedom of speech. I care if you’re breaking the law," Slotkin told CNN. PENNSYLVANIA SOCIALIST DEMOCRAT SAYS HE OPPOSES IMPRISONMENT EXCEPT FOR 'LAWLESS MAGA THUGS' During a separate interview on MS NOW, Slotkin suggested some of the backlash she received from Republican critics could be attributed to her gender. "I think when you choose to call out their corruption, they clearly don't like that," Slotkin said on MS NOW's "Deadline: White House." "They're clearly trying to change the conversation given what the midterms are and the state of the economy, the state of things around the country. I do think there's something about being a woman and criticizing them and calling them out on that corruption that really gets under their skin, obviously, or they wouldn't respond." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When reached for comment, Slotkin's office directed Fox News Digital to her comments in the MS NOW interview.
news.summary: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., dismissed criticism on CNN as "manufactured outrage" after her viral remarks about prosecuting Trump administration enablers.

news.title: Who gets a share of AI wealth? Anthropic and Musk have different answers
news.text:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude family of AI models, said on Sunday that it would commit 5 per cent of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund. Musk, meanwhile, pledged on Monday to give one SpaceX share to every child in America next year.
The proposals come as AI companies attract huge investments and expand their businesses, while concerns grow over the technology's impact on jobs, safety and society.
The difference lies in how the two plans would work. Anthropic's fund could finance charitable initiatives and potentially make direct payments to selected groups. Musk has said that giving shares directly to people is a better way to let the public participate in the future economy.
Anthropic's fund could be worth billions
Anthropic's proposed fund could be worth tens of billions of dollars, depending on the company's valuation.
The AI firm is preparing for a potential initial public offering (IPO) that could value it at around $2 trillion. Reuters reported last week that some investors were also considering a lower valuation of about $1.5 trillion.
At those valuations, a 5 per cent stake would be worth between $75 billion and $100 billion. These are estimates based on potential valuations, not cash that Anthropic has already raised for the fund.
The company said the fund would be established as a wholly owned limited liability company, giving it flexibility to support different public-benefit initiatives. These could include large donations to non-profit organisations or direct distributions to specific groups of people.
One area of focus could be the labour market. Anthropic has warned that AI could create enormous economic value but also disrupt jobs and cause instability for workers.
The company has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing the effects of AI on employment. It said the new fund could allow it to take further steps as the technology develops.
Anthropic also plans to give the fund the option of receiving more shares as the company grows. Its board could allocate an additional 2 per cent of the company's shares for every 50 per cent increase in its value above a baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
The company said the fund would not use its Anthropic shares for lobbying or political donations in the United States or abroad.
The new commitment builds on earlier pledges by Anthropic's founders and employees. The co-founders had pledged to donate 80 per cent of their equity holdings, while an employee donation-matching programme allows workers to pledge shares that the company matches.
Anthropic said roughly 20 per cent of its shares would be dedicated to public-benefit purposes when these commitments are combined, excluding any additional shares that may later go to the fund.
The company has yet to disclose the fund's full governance structure and the valuation thresholds that could increase its stake.
Musk plans to give SpaceX shares to children
Musk said on Monday that he would give one SpaceX share to every child in America next year, describing the move as the first of several such efforts.
Based on US Census figures showing about 72 million children in the country, the proposed distribution could be worth roughly $11 billion at current share prices.
Musk did not provide details on how the shares would be distributed, which children would qualify or whether recipients would face restrictions on selling them.
SpaceX also did not immediately clarify whether the proposed giveaway would be linked to Trump Accounts, a US government-backed investment programme for children.
Launched by the White House, Trump Accounts provide a government-funded $1,000 investment account for eligible US citizens born between 2025 and 2028. Families can add money to the accounts as the children grow up.
The programme also allows companies and individuals to contribute to the accounts. Dell, Visa, Micron and Delta Air Lines are among the companies that have pledged additional funding or employer contributions.
US President Donald Trump welcomed Musk's announcement, thanking him on Truth Social for giving SpaceX stock to millions of American children through the programme.
Unlike a cash donation, the value of Musk's proposed contribution would depend on SpaceX's share price. Recipients could benefit if the stock rises, but the value of their holdings could also fall.
Musk has argued that direct share ownership would allow people to benefit from the growth of companies shaping the future economy.
Why AI companies are under pressure to share wealth
The announcements come as AI's rapid growth brings both financial opportunities and concerns about its wider effects.
Businesses are adopting AI tools to improve productivity and reduce costs. Some companies, particularly in the technology sector, have announced job cuts while pointing to efficiency gains from the technology.
Anthropic has also warned that advanced AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Its proposed fund could support initiatives addressing some of these concerns, including the effects of automation on workers.
The wider question is whether the gains from AI will remain concentrated among companies, founders and investors or reach a larger share of society.
Anthropic's approach would direct part of its ownership towards a fund that can finance public-benefit projects. Musk's proposal would give children a direct financial stake in SpaceX, exposing the value of their holdings to the company's future performance.
Neither initiative has yet provided all the details needed to assess how much the public will ultimately receive or how the benefits will be distributed.
Anthropic still needs to explain the fund's governance and how its additional share commitments will work. Musk has not outlined the mechanics of his proposed giveaway.

news.title: CNBC Daily Open: Tech investors buy the dip — but debt remains a concern
news.text:
Business News and FinanceVIEW IN APPMarketsBusinessInvestingTechPoliticsSelectMake ItDaily OpenCNBC Daily Open: Tech investors buy the dip — but debt remains a concernPublished Mon, Oct 19 2026 9:11 PM EDTUpdated 14 Min AgoLim Hui Jie@in/hui-jie-lim-a7371176/WATCH LIVEKEY POINTS The Nasdaq Composite rebounds after a week of bruising losses. Oracle bonds inch closer to junk territory. Anthropic seen as the last AI IPO that could happen for 2026. Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine continue to rise. Elon Musk says he’ll give a SpaceX share to every child in AmericaIn this article

Hello, this is Hui Jie writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.

After a bruising week for the tech trade, investors seem to have came back into the sector, with the Nasdaq Composite rallying overnight.

The optimism is cautious, with debt concerns still a key worry for a sector that has seen record bond issuance this year.

Investors are once again piling into tech, after fears over AI financing, rising competition and possible excess chip supply in a few years drove them to cash out of the market last week.

The Nasdaq Composite rebounded more than 1% on Monday, after sliding 4.5% last week and snapping a four-week winning streak.

Intel advanced 2% after JPMorgan analysts upgraded their rating on the chipmaker. Advanced Micro Devices added 1.8%, and Micron Technology jumped about 3%.

It was not a wholesale embrace of the sector, however. Funding concerns still loom, especially over neocloud companies.

Shares of neocloud mainstay CoreWeave reversed course from earlier gains, falling 0.4%, even after receiving Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to buy from neutral.

CoreWeave shares plunged more than 25% last week — their biggest one-week drop since November 2025 — over debt concerns.

Another company that is also facing credit stress is Oracle. It risks a credit rating downgrade that could tip its debt into junk territory. Oracle's rating at S&P Credit Ratings is BBB-, the lowest level in the investment-grade spectrum.

While the bonds are still investment grade, the shift in sentiment can be seen in the spread of Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default.

Oracle's five-year CDS spread, or premium, is currently at 295 basis points, after briefly hitting 300 basis points on Thursday. It is up 287% in one year.

The range is more in line with BB and B credit, which is high yield, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

When the year started, investors were predicting a slew of AI companies going public, including SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI.

But now investors will have to settle for less, with OpenAI ruling out its market debut in 2026 and several other planned offerings postponed this year.

On prediction market platform Kalshi, speculators think the only major company left that might officially announce an IPO this year is Anthropic, which confidentially filed a prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in early June.

Only Anthropic offers greater than 50% odds — 75% as of Monday morning — to officially announce an IPO this year, out of the 23 companies that Kalshi lists on its market that remain open to trade.

On the geopolitical front, the tensions between Washington and Kyiv continue to rise with President Donald Trump saying Monday he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss how to end the Ukraine war.

That comes after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump had floated the idea of a trilateral summit with Xi next month, although the meeting is envisioned to exclude Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump told reporters when asked about the potential meeting as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.

Trump also doubled down on his criticism of the Ukrainian leader when he was asked about Zelenskyy's remarks that Trump is on the wrong side of history, saying that "Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," and reiterating his call for Kyiv to "get a new president."

Elon Musk says he’ll give a SpaceX share to every child in America next year

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.

Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.

There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.

That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.
